steps: The three domains that encompass all living organisms are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
items.finalAnswer: The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

steps: Viruses are acellular and do not have the cellular organisation of organisms in the kingdoms.
They cannot carry out life processes or reproduce independently; they reproduce only inside a living host cell.
Therefore, viruses cannot be placed in any kingdom.
items.finalAnswer: Viruses are acellular and reproduce only inside host cells, so they cannot be classified in any kingdom.

steps: In binomial nomenclature, each organism is given a two-part scientific name: the genus name followed by the species name.
Scientific names are standardised and generally written in Latin or Latinised form.
The same scientific name is used worldwide, avoiding confusion caused by different common names in different languages.
items.finalAnswer: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a standard, universally used scientific name, avoiding language-based confusion.

steps: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms found in an area or on Earth, including the variety of species, genes and ecosystems.
Organisms in an ecosystem are connected through food chains and other interactions.
Biodiversity helps ecosystems remain balanced, productive and resilient to environmental changes.
Living organisms provide important ecosystem services, such as pollination, nutrient cycling and the supply of food and other resources.
A loss of biodiversity can disrupt these interactions and make ecosystems less healthy.
items.finalAnswer: Biodiversity supports ecosystem balance, resilience and essential services, helping maintain ecosystem health.

steps: Classification is the systematic arrangement of organisms into groups on the basis of their similarities and differences.
It makes the study of the great variety of organisms easier and more organised.
It helps in identifying and naming organisms and in comparing their characteristics.
The classification groups show relationships among organisms; organisms placed in closer groups share more characteristics and have closer relationships.
items.finalAnswer: Classification organises organisms for easier study and identification, and shows how they are related.

steps: The Linnaean system classifies organisms into a hierarchy of groups called taxa, from the broadest group to the most specific.
The seven taxonomic ranks, in descending order, are kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
Each kingdom is divided into phyla; each phylum into classes; each class into orders; each order into families; each family into genera; and each genus into species.
A species is the most specific rank, while a kingdom is the broadest of these seven ranks.
As we move from kingdom towards species, the groups become smaller and their members share more characteristics.
items.finalAnswer: The Linnaean hierarchy is kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species, from broadest to most specific.

steps: Archaea and Bacteria are both domains of unicellular prokaryotes; their cells have no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.
Bacteria are found in a wide range of environments, and many are familiar organisms such as those found in soil, water and living things.
Archaea are often associated with extreme environments, although they also occur in other habitats.
Their cell walls differ: bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan, while archaeal cell walls do not.
Archaea also differ from bacteria in the chemical composition of their cell membranes and in some aspects of their genetic machinery.
items.finalAnswer: Archaea and Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotes, but differ in cell-wall and membrane chemistry, genetic machinery and common habitats.

steps: The domain Eukarya includes organisms whose cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Kingdom Protista: mostly unicellular eukaryotes; some are plant-like and photosynthetic, while others are animal-like and obtain food from other sources.
Kingdom Fungi: eukaryotes that usually have cell walls and obtain nutrients by absorption; they include yeasts, moulds and mushrooms.
Kingdom Plantae: multicellular eukaryotes that have cell walls and chlorophyll and make their food by photosynthesis.
Kingdom Animalia: multicellular eukaryotes that lack cell walls and obtain food by consuming other organisms; most can move from place to place.
items.finalAnswer: Eukarya includes Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, distinguished by their organisation and methods of obtaining food.
